message.content:
The wind was a raw, salt-crusted fist against the granite tower. Elias, the lighthouse keeper, had grown deaf to its howl, but not to the rhythm of the sea. On his morning patrol of the rocky cove, a glint of green caught his eye—a bottle, wedged between two barnacle-encrusted boulders.

He pried it loose, the glass cold and slick. Inside, a curl of paper, yellowed and brittle. With the careful hands of a man used to delicate mechanisms, he worked the cork free and coaxed the message out.

The ink was faded, the handwriting a frantic scrawl. *“My darling, the storm has taken our rudder. We are drifting. I think of your lighthouse, of the warm light in the kitchen window. Tell our son I love him. Tell him to be brave. I will find my way home by the stars you keep.”*

It was signed with a single initial: *M.*

Elias read it three times. He knew every ship that had been lost in these waters for forty years. He knew every name carved into the granite memorial above the cliff. There was no *M* he could recall. No son who had come asking.

He looked from the paper to the endless, churning grey. The message was a ghost, a moment of terror and love frozen in time, finally washing ashore decades too late.

Elias did not throw it back. He climbed the winding stairs to the lantern room, his joints aching. He placed the bottle on the sill, where the great beam of light would catch it each night. He could not guide the ship home, but he could keep its last, desperate love alight.
